title: What Real Discipleship Looks Like
subtitle: Moving the local church beyond programs and curriculum to the slow work of forming whole people who actually follow Jesus

sections.title: Not a Program. A Person Formed.
sections.body:
We have spent a generation building discipleship programs. Curricula, tracks, six-week studies, app reminders, a path with stations a person can be moved through. And we have produced people who can pass a quiz on the faith and cannot forgive their brother.

Discipleship is not information transfer. It is the slow remaking of a human being into the likeness of Christ.

A program assumes the problem is that people do not know enough. Sometimes that is true. More often the problem is that what they know has never reached their hands and their tempers and their checkbooks and their marriages. The Pharisees knew the most. Jesus called them the furthest gone. So if your church measures discipleship by how much content a person has consumed, you may be running the very machine that produces well-informed people who do not love. Real discipleship asks a harder question. Not what do they know. Who are they becoming.

sections.title: How Jesus Actually Did It
sections.body:
Jesus could have written a curriculum. He had the authority to dictate the perfect course. Instead he called twelve men to follow him around for three years and watch how he lived.

He ate with them. He was tired in front of them. He let them see him weep, see him angry, see him pray when he thought he was alone.

This is the part our programs cannot reproduce, because it cannot be scaled and cannot be photographed. Formation happens through proximity to a life. Paul said it without flinching. Follow my example as I follow Christ. We have lost the nerve to say that. We hand people a book instead of a life because a book asks nothing of us and a shared life asks everything. But no one was ever discipled by a curriculum. They were discipled by a person whose faith they could watch up close, on good days and bad, until it became plausible that they could live that way too.

sections.title: The Whole Person, Not the Sunday Self
sections.body:
A disciple is not formed for one hour on Sunday. A disciple is formed for the Tuesday afternoon when no one is watching and the temptation is real and the choice is made alone.

If your discipleship only touches what a person believes and never what a person does at the kitchen table, it is not discipleship. It is decoration.

The test of formation is not the worship service. It is the marriage, the parenting, the way a man treats the waitress, the way a woman talks about the people who are not in the room. James K. A. Smith has spent his career arguing that we are formed less by what we think than by what we love and what we practice, by the habits that shape our loves while we are not paying attention. He is right, and the church has been slow to hear it. We aimed at the head and left the heart to whatever the culture was already discipling it toward. And the culture disciples relentlessly, all week, while we get one hour.

sections.title: Why It Costs You More Than a Class
sections.body:
Here is why we prefer programs. They let us disciple a hundred people while knowing none of them. Real discipleship cannot be done at that distance.

It requires that you let a few people close enough to see your real life. That is expensive, and it is why so little of it happens.

Jesus poured most of his three years into twelve, and most of that into three. The pastor who tries to personally form everyone forms no one, and the pastor who forms no one because it is more efficient to teach the crowd has chosen the crowd over the work. I have done both. I have hidden in the size of the room. I have preferred the audience that asks nothing intimate of me to the handful who would actually watch how I live. The verdict on my own ministry is partly written there. Discipleship is not a thing you broadcast. It is a thing you hand over, in person, at cost, to the few you can actually reach.

sections.title: Discipleship Has an Address
sections.body:
Real discipleship is not abstract, and it does not happen in the air. It happens somewhere specific, at a particular table, between particular people, on a Tuesday that is not special.

It happens over coffee that goes cold while a man finally says the thing he has never told anyone. It happens in a car on the way home from the hospital. It happens in a kitchen.

We keep trying to systematize what only ever moves through relationship, because systems are safe and relationships are not. A system cannot be hurt by you. A person can. But the trade Jesus invites is exactly that vulnerable exchange, your real life for theirs, watched and shared at close range over years. Eugene Peterson spent decades insisting that pastoral work is local, particular, and slow, that it resists the impatience of a culture addicted to scale. He was describing discipleship. It has an address. It has a name. It is not a movement you join. It is a few people you let close enough to change you, and whom you let yourself change in return.

sections.title: What You Will Actually See
sections.body:
So what does a discipled church look like. Not a building full of people who finished the course. A building full of people who are visibly changing in the places change is hardest.

You will see a temper losing its grip. A marriage being repaired. A grudge laid down. A wallet opening. A tongue learning to bless.

These are unglamorous, unphotographable, slow. They will never trend. They are the only evidence that matters. A church can run flawless programs for a decade and produce no one who is more like Jesus, and it can run almost nothing and produce saints, if the few who lead are genuinely being formed and are genuinely letting others close. Stop asking how many completed the track. Start asking who is becoming kind, becoming patient, becoming brave, becoming holy. That is the fruit. Everything else is scaffolding, and scaffolding was never the building.
